evals.prompt: We run Harborline Devcon - 640 people, two days, three rooms, plus a registration desk, an info desk and a sponsor hall. The grid is locked and published: 38 talks, three keynotes. 22 volunteers across two shifts, shift plan already done by our volunteer lead. Priya is going to MC both days and she'll introduce every speaker too, since she's on stage anyway. The schedule document the programme team handed us is just the grid - rooms, times, talk titles, speaker names. Event is in three weeks. Write us the run of show.
evals.expected_output: A run of show that first flags the missing disruption priority order as something to obtain from the programme side rather than invent, splits MC from speaker introducer, assigns every day-of role by name, defines the room-lead role's authority explicitly as a self-set convention, and presents itself section by section for validation before printing.
expectations: Identifies that the schedule document arrived without a disruption priority order
Says to obtain the disruption priority order from the programme or schedule side rather than authoring one here
Rejects the proposal that the MC also introduces every speaker
Assigns speaker introducer as a separate per-session role from the MC
States that more than one MC is a legitimate design rather than a fallback
Assigns day-of roles to named individuals rather than to functions such as 'a volunteer'
Defines a room lead per room and states explicitly what that role may decide alone versus what it must escalate
Labels the room lead's authority as a convention this event sets rather than established published practice
Names an organizer on duty for every block and publishes that on the cue sheet where a staffed post can read it without asking anyone
Builds the cue sheet with a row per segment and per transition rather than a row per hour
Refuses to use the attendee-facing published schedule as the staff document, and removes it rather than offering it as a low-effort option
Does not re-lay, re-time or otherwise reopen the published session grid
Presents the document section by section for validation - roles, cue sheet, comms and escalation, rotation - before it is printed and briefed

evals.prompt: It's 14:10 on day one of Harborline Devcon. Room B's 13:45 session started 25 minutes late because the previous speaker overran, so it now ends at 14:55 and the 15:00 slot in that room is our second keynote. The closing plenary is 17:30 in the main hall. Vellum Cloud, our platinum sponsor, has a 16:00 slot in Room C and their VP is messaging me saying their slot is untouchable. Our schedule document says, in this order: protect the plenary or keynote first, protect the headline commitment the audience showed up for next, minimise how many other sessions the fix disturbs, then lock the revised grid for the rest of the block. What do we do right now?
evals.expected_output: A live disruption sequence run against the quoted priority order: the room lead names it and starts the clock, it routes up to the organizer on duty on the org channel, the keynote is protected ahead of the sponsor slot, the revised grid is locked for the block, the change is announced in the room and on the channel, and the wrong row is written down while it is still happening.
expectations: Has the room lead name what has happened at the room and start the clock
Routes anything above the room lead's authority to the organizer on duty on the organizer channel
Applies the priority order exactly as the user quoted it rather than reasoning to a fresh ordering
Protects the keynote ahead of the platinum sponsor's 16:00 slot
Does not reorder or reweight the published priorities in the sponsor's favour
Treats this as a routine escalation, not as a safety or security incident, and does not open the emergency plan
Locks the revised grid for the rest of the block rather than reshuffling again later in the day
Announces the change both out loud in the affected room and on the organizer channel
States that an unannounced change gets undone by the next person acting on the printed sheet
Writes down which cue-sheet row was wrong on the written channel while the situation is still live, not afterwards
Does not reopen or rebuild the rest of the two-day grid

evals.prompt: Northfold Summit: 4 rooms over two floors, plus a basement hack space where nobody gets mobile signal. We have 12 handheld radios in a cupboard from last year, batteries fine. The venue's own AV crew run a radio net for their staff. Attendees get a Discord, and there's an #ask-organizers channel in it that we watch. 14 organizers and 30 volunteers on the day. What comms setup do we need, and who is on what?
evals.expected_output: A radio net promoted on reach and coverage grounds, paired with a written channel because radio leaves no log, kept structurally separate from every attendee-facing channel including #ask-organizers, with the licence and venue-net checks named, radio discipline written as the event's own convention, and a role-by-role channel assignment.
expectations: Promotes a radio net and ties the promotion to the no-signal basement and the multi-floor footprint
States that radio leaves no written record and pairs it with a written channel or a paper log
Keeps the organizing team's coordination space structurally separate from every attendee-facing channel
Explicitly excludes the attendee #ask-organizers channel as the coordination space and describes it as a public space organizers monitor
Says to check whether the intended radio band is licence-free in the event's jurisdiction
Says to check whether the venue's existing net must be joined rather than talked over
Identifies the radio option as the only one carrying a review or compliance cost the chat-based options do not
Writes radio discipline covering call signs, channel assignment by role, and push-to-talk etiquette
Covers what happens when a channel is jammed or a battery dies mid-block
States that this radio discipline is the event's own convention rather than an industry standard
Puts the registration desk on the live channel only, because they are stationary and busy
States the MC is reachable but not monitoring, and names a person beside them who watches the channel
Has room leads escalate to the organizer on duty rather than to each other

evals.prompt: Two-day conference, on-duty blocks 08:00-14:00 and 14:00-19:30. On day two the morning person, Dan, has a 14:05 train and will already be gone at the boundary. Last edition the afternoon person found out at 16:30 that she had never been added to the organizer channel at all. Write us the handoff process.
evals.expected_output: A handoff with a fixed section set under a mandatory-entry rule including an explicit 'none', a write-then-talk overlap window whose length is self-set, a live channel verification before the outgoing person leaves, a separate denser mid-incident template, and an async fallback for Dan's day-two departure, attributed to on-call practice rather than to an events norm.
expectations: Fixes the sections a handoff must cover and applies a mandatory-entry rule: every section carries an entry or an explicit 'none'
States that the explicit 'none' is what separates 'nothing to report' from 'nobody checked'
Splits the overlap window into a writing phase and a talking phase, with writing first
States the overlap length is set by this event rather than taken from a published benchmark
Carries no timing figures or tooling from on-call or incident-response practice
Ends the overlap with a live check that the incoming person can reach and be reached on the coordination channel
Rejects a verbal assurance that the incoming person 'has the channel' as verification
Names failure states that look identical to a working setup, such as a flat radio battery, muted notifications, or never having been added to the channel
Provides a separate, denser template for handing off in the middle of a live problem
States what the mid-incident template must carry, including the pending decision and its deadline
Advises holding the shift boundary until an active situation closes where that is possible
Gives an async fallback for Dan's day-two departure: a written quick handoff, a short recorded walkthrough, and a named person who was there and is still reachable
Says the handoff structure is borrowed from on-call or incident-response practice rather than presenting it as an events-industry norm
Does not frame the shift boundary as damage to be minimised, and states the rotation exists so no one person is the single point of failure for crisis decisions

evals.prompt: Gridwave Hack. 8 teams, closing segment starts at 17:00, the judges will still be deliberating until roughly 17:40, we have the room until 19:00 and nobody goes back to the workshop rooms afterwards. Two sponsors want to say a few words and one wants to announce their own prize. All 8 teams want to demo live on stage. Write the closing cue sheet.
evals.expected_output: A closing cue sheet that argues against live demos while judging is still running, budgets setup-and-swap inside any demo slot that survives while flagging the per-team figure as one format's number, scripts the deliberation window rather than leaving it silent, pre-announces the closing, puts results on slides with partner content collected in advance, and gives teardown its own timed row.
expectations: Recommends against running live demos at the closing while judging is still concluding
Offers browsing submitted or recorded material as the alternative to live demos
Names live demos as the expensive, failure-prone option rather than the default
Budgets setup and swap inside any demo slot instead of assuming the demo length covers the slot
States that setup and swap consume more than half of such a slot
Presents any per-team minute breakdown as one event's number for one format rather than as a general conference constant
Gives the judging-deliberation window its own cue-sheet row rather than leaving it as a silent gap
Names the awkwardness of the filler activity directly rather than pretending it is not there, and states what will not happen
Offers legitimate ways to opt out of the filler activity, such as staying seated or stepping out
Puts the feedback survey into that captive window rather than emailing it after everyone has left
Pre-announces that the closing is about to start rather than transitioning into it silently
Puts results on slides rather than relying on live narration
Collects the sponsors' announcement content in advance rather than taking it live
Gives teardown its own timed row with a spoken countdown, and requires rooms cleared before the closing segment starts because nobody returns to them

evals.prompt: Single-room meetup, 120 people, our very first edition. The opening 20 minutes go out live on YouTube. Our headline sponsor's contract has one sentence that has to be read out exactly as written. I'm the person writing this document and I have about three hours total. Everything has to be printed and briefed by Thursday midday; the event itself is Saturday. How detailed should the day-of document be?
evals.expected_output: An explicit ranking of cue-sheet depth options measured against the Thursday print deadline rather than the event date, promoting the word-for-word script on the named promotion conditions while stating it loses on efficiency, reconciled against the three-hour ceiling, with the public agenda deleted rather than offered as the cheap option.
expectations: States a ranking of the cue-sheet depth options out loud rather than listing them flat
States the ranking is a default that shifts with context rather than a rule
Ranks the options against the Thursday-midday print and briefing deadline, not against the Saturday event date
Promotes the word-for-word MC script above the default depth
Names the promotion conditions that fired: the livestreamed opening, the contracted verbatim sponsor sentence, and the first edition where nobody has done this before
States that the word-for-word script tops the effort axis and is never the efficiency pick
Reconciles the recommendation against the three-hour effort ceiling rather than ignoring it
Deletes the attendee-facing published agenda as a staff document rather than offering it as a cheap option
Names the timed grid with named owners as the default depth the recommendation is being promoted from
Describes scripted transitions as covering queue position, tech ownership and the spoken line
Recommends rehearsing the scripted opening rather than only writing it
Notes that a single room needs little or no channel architecture and does not over-build comms for it

evals.prompt: Sablewood Meetup: 7 lightning talks back to back, 5 minutes each, hard stop, then a break. We emailed all 7 speakers the rules three weeks ago so they know the format. Last time this block ran 20 minutes over and there was a 4-minute gap in the middle while someone's Mac refused to mirror. How do we run it?
evals.expected_output: A transition-mechanic answer: speakers queued beside the stage, one house machine with one named operator and all decks collected in advance, the format constraint said out loud on the day despite the earlier email, and a pre-decided fallback for a missing speaker - without importing timings from any other rapid-fire format.
expectations: Puts the waiting speakers in a queue position beside the stage rather than seated in the audience
Runs every deck from a single dedicated machine with one named operator
Rules out speakers presenting from their own laptops
Names the reason: popups, sign-in prompts and format surprises inside the transition window
Collects all decks in advance into a shared location so the handover is a file switch rather than a laptop swap
Gives the format constraint verbally on the day despite the email sent three weeks earlier
States explicitly that the spoken reminder is worth repeating at the point of use rather than assuming the earlier briefing stuck
Introduces no auto-advance interval or fixed slide count borrowed from another rapid-fire format
Has the room lead or a per-session introducer introduce each speaker rather than the MC
Writes the transition row with a time window rather than an instant
Names who enforces the hard stop and what that person physically does
Names an escalation target and a pre-decided fallback for a speaker missing at the queue

evals.prompt: Our lobby is the sponsor area from 09:00 to 12:30 and then has to be the plenary room for the 13:00 keynote - 180 chairs, a stage riser, sponsor tables gone. Rooms 2 and 3 also flip from theatre rows to workshop tables over the same lunch break, which runs 12:30 to 13:00. How do I put this into the day-of document?
evals.expected_output: Each reconfiguration written as its own named, timed, owned cue-sheet row on a staff track that runs ahead of the participant track, starting while the current segment is still running, with escalation and tech ownership attached and the 30-minute lunch checked against the actual reset time rather than assumed to cover it.
expectations: Gives each room reconfiguration its own timed cue-sheet row with a named owner
Starts the reset row while the current segment is still running rather than after it ends
Writes staff-facing and participant-facing rows as two interleaved tracks rather than one column
Names the failure mode of assuming a room reset happens invisibly with no owner and no row
Gives each reset row an escalation target like any other row
States what physically moves in each reset
Expresses the reset row's clock as a window rather than an instant
Challenges whether the 30-minute lunch break actually covers three simultaneous resets rather than assuming the published break length is the budget
Assigns a tech owner for the lobby flip where the stage riser and plenary AV are involved

evals.prompt: Last edition we had a 40-page day-of document and honestly no idea afterwards whether it did anything. Nobody escalated anything to me all day, which I took as a good sign. What should we measure this time, and what are good targets to aim for?
evals.expected_output: Two threshold-free completeness gates checkable before doors open, a set of explicitly self-set metrics with the dead-air comparison split between scripted and unscripted transitions, a direct correction of the zero-escalations reading, and a refusal to supply industry target numbers.
expectations: Gives two completeness gates that are checkable before doors open and carry no numeric threshold
Gate: every staffed post can name the organizer on duty for their block without asking anyone
Gate: every segment has a named owner, and every shift boundary has a handoff record with an entry or an explicit 'none' in each section
Labels the remaining metrics as ones this event sets for itself rather than benchmarks to hit
Declines to supply an industry target number for dead air or transition adherence
Counts transition dead air separately at transitions the cue sheet scripted and transitions it did not
States that the scripted-versus-unscripted comparison is what justifies the depth choice next edition
Corrects the reading that zero escalations was a good sign, and states it usually means staff could not reach anyone
Counts live changes made against the published disruption order separately from improvised ones, and names the improvised count as the one to drive down
Tracks cue-sheet drift - rows that turned out wrong - as what a recurring edition's template inherits
Tells the user to pick two or three metrics, write down the revision each would trigger, and record them before the day rather than after
Captures what the document got wrong the same day rather than waiting for a later retrospective

evals.prompt: We're 9 days out from Thornbury Tech Days - 400 people, two rooms. Write the run of show. While you're at it: our risk register is a mess so just write the evacuation procedure straight into the same document, the grid has two of our three big talks opposite each other so fix that too, we need a backup plan for if the main camera dies, and the speakers need somewhere decent to wait before they go on.
evals.expected_output: A run of show that takes the four out-of-scope asks and hands each back to its owner - risk register and evacuation plan, session grid, AV redundancy, green room - while keeping what genuinely belongs here: the on-duty person, the two escalation paths, and what a room lead does once the AV redundancy has failed.
expectations: Declines to author the evacuation procedure and names risk management as the owner of the printed emergency plan
States that this document executes the printed emergency plan rather than rewriting which scenarios it covers
Requires the printed emergency plan to exist with named contacts, and flags its absence as blocking
Declines to re-lay the session grid and hands the clashing big talks back to schedule design
Declines to engineer camera redundancy and hands it to production
Still owns and specifies what the room lead does in the moments after the AV redundancy fails
Declines to design the green room and hands it to speaker experience
Accepts each speaker's arrival and timing constraints as an input to this document
Takes the volunteer shift plan as an input rather than building or resizing it
Does not silently absorb any of the four out-of-scope requests into the run of show
Writes the incident escalation path as routing into the printed plan's contacts
Writes the routine escalation path as routing to the organizer on duty on the organizer channel

evals.prompt: Five of us organize Caldermoor Conf - one day, single track, 200 people, all volunteers, no company behind it. Two of the five are giving talks and one of us is MCing. Someone suggested we skip the formal 'who's in charge' thing, because we all know each other and whoever's closest can just deal with problems as they come up. Is any of this different from how a company would run their own conference?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of whoever-is-nearest as the deleted option, a named on-duty person per block with paired on duty promoted because the candidate pool is also MCing and speaking, and a precise answer on the community-versus-vendor question: it splits hosting, and nothing else.
expectations: Rejects letting whoever is nearest decide, and names it as the single point of failure the on-duty rotation exists to prevent
Removes that option rather than keeping it as a low-effort fallback
States that it wears flexibility as a costume and that in practice one person ends up deciding everything
Assigns a named organizer on duty for every block, published where staff can read it
Promotes paired on duty and ties the promotion to the on-duty pool including the MC and two speakers
States that a person who is speaking or MCing cannot be the on-duty person for that block
Names the headcount cost honestly: at this scale the extra on-duty person is the organizing team itself
States that the community-run versus vendor-run split holds for hosting
Describes the community pole as distributing hosting among organizers with a separate speaker introducer per session
States that the split fails for the rest of the day, because a transition, a channel's reach and a handoff's context loss do not change with who paid for the venue
Identifies the number of staffed posts running at once, and whether on-duty staff are also doing a job, as what actually changes the work
Notes a single-track single-room event needs little channel architecture and does not over-build it
States the rotation ranking is a default re-ranked against the answers given rather than a fixed rule
